title: Philly suburb: Sure, build that data center—but first meet our 43 demands
gist: Plymouth Township outside Philadelphia responded to a proposed 2 million-square-foot data center on a former steel plant with a 43-point, nine-page condition list requiring on-site power generation instead of public utilities, closed-loop non-potable cooling, decommissioning bonds, prevailing wages and a covenant not to appeal taxes. Developer Brian O’Neill, who wants six data centers in the area, is now challenging the zoning ordinance as effectively prohibitory, and the township calls the challenge approval by tantrum.

themes.theme: Conditions as a de facto veto

insights.claim: Under Pennsylvania law Plymouth Township cannot simply refuse a lawful land use, but it can enforce zoning rules and require mitigations for health and safety, so conditions become the only available instrument of local resistance.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Where outright denial is unlawful, condition stacking is the mechanism to watch for data center siting risk nationally.
insights.locator: Under Pennsylvania law, Plymouth Township

insights.claim: Plymouth Township produced a 43-point plan covering nine printed pages after the developer's company represented it would implement any provisions the township proposed.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Blanket pre-agreement to unspecified conditions is a negotiating trap developers keep walking into.
insights.locator: According to the township, O’Neill’s company

insights.claim: The author's general framing is that developers express willingness to pay taxes, cover water and power upgrades, limit noise and hire locally until they see the specific list of requirements.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: The gap between stated community-benefit willingness and signed conditions is where data center project delays originate.
insights.quote: Developers often express a willingness to do these things—until they see the specific list of requirements.
insights.locator: From New York to Texas, state and local governments

insights.claim: Across the political spectrum large numbers of Americans agree data centers should pay taxes, cover water and power upgrade bills, minimize noise and employ locals at decent wages, making this a bipartisan constraint rather than a partisan one.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Bipartisan opposition means data center siting friction will not be resolved by an election outcome.
insights.locator: From New York to Texas, state and local governments have heard the message

insights.claim: The township requires the data center to be power self-sufficient through on-site generation and to not use public utilities to power the project at all, the single most economically consequential condition on the list.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Forcing behind-the-meter generation transforms data center capex and favors developers with gas turbine or fuel cell capability.
insights.locator: The site must be “power self-su

insights.claim: The site must attempt to use renewable power generation with a stated preference for solar to the greatest extent possible, and must deploy a clean air micro-grid or a combined heat and power system to address emissions.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Micro-grid and CHP mandates create a local procurement market for distributed generation vendors as the price of siting approval.
insights.quote: attempt to utilize renewable power generation technology, with a preference for solar power, to the greatest extent possible
insights.locator: The site must be “power self-su

insights.claim: Cooling must use a closed-loop system with non-toxic coolant that cannot be drawn from any public system or discharged into a watercourse, sewer system or in a manner that could contaminate groundwater.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Closed-loop non-potable cooling mandates raise capex and rule out the cheapest evaporative designs.
insights.locator: For cooling, the site must use a “closed loop” system

insights.claim: The developer must file an annual water consumption report and may not draw water from the Schuylkill River or any public water system except for restrooms and kitchens, nor discharge into the river.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Water rights are being ring-fenced explicitly, a template other watershed municipalities can copy verbatim.
insights.locator: An annual water consumption report is required

insights.claim: A thermal impact plan must identify all proposed sources of waste heat in both air and water, show mitigation and shielding, and reuse waste heat where possible.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Waste heat reuse mandates are migrating from European practice into US local zoning conditions.
insights.locator: A thermal impact plan must identify all proposed sources of waste heat

insights.claim: The township requires pre-construction and post-construction noise studies establishing baseline ambient noise and vibration at different times of day, with ongoing compliance especially at low frequencies, plus parapet sound walls screening rooftop machinery.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Low-frequency noise compliance is the technically hardest data center condition and a recurring source of post-build litigation.
insights.locator: A pre-construction noise study must be done

insights.claim: The site may not produce any perceptible vibration causing recurring rattling of nearby windows, walls, floors, ceilings or household contents, and all electronic equipment must be shielded so no radio or television interference is discernible at the property boundary.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Perceptibility-based standards are subjective and give the township continuing enforcement leverage after construction.
insights.locator: The site may also not have “any perceptible vibration level

insights.claim: Buildings on the site may not exceed two occupiable stories, a severe constraint on fitting 2 million square feet of data center onto the former steel plant parcel.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Height caps force horizontal sprawl and can make a proposed square footage physically infeasible on the site.
insights.locator: Buildings on the site shall not exceed two occupiable stories.

insights.claim: Exterior lighting must meet Dark Sky Standards and trees and shrubs must buffer any part of the property abutting residential areas for both noise abatement and visual screening.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Standardized lighting and buffer requirements are the low-cost conditions developers concede first in negotiations.
insights.locator: Exterior lights must meet Dark Sky Standards.

insights.claim: The data center must recruit local workers and commit to paying prevailing wage and benefit rates, importing a public-works labor standard into a private development approval.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: Prevailing-wage conditions raise construction cost materially and are a growing template in data center siting fights.
insights.quote: commit to paying prevailing wage and benefit rates
insights.locator: The data center must recruit local workers

insights.claim: No permits will be issued until the developer posts financial security equal to the full cost of decommissioning, held by the township until released, alongside a decommissioning plan on file.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: A full decommissioning bond is a large upfront cash drag and directly attacks data center project IRR.
insights.quote: financial security [in] the amount equal to the cost of decommissioning, which shall be held until released by the Township
insights.locator: The site must have a full “decommissioning plan” on file.

insights.claim: The developer must provide assurances that it will pay all taxes and shall not attempt to reduce the tax burden owed to the township, contractually foreclosing the standard assessment-appeal playbook.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: A covenant against tax appeals is unusual and, if enforceable, removes a core lever data center operators use to cut opex.
insights.quote: shall not attempt to reduce the tax burden owed to the Township
insights.locator: Finally, the developer must provide assurances

insights.claim: Developer Brian O’Neill's lawyers are challenging the township zoning ordinance on grounds the conditions have become too burdensome to develop the 2 million-square-foot facility on the former steel plant.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: The legal challenge converts a siting negotiation into precedent-setting litigation on how far conditions can go.
insights.locator: His lawyers are now challenging the township’s zoning ordinance

insights.claim: Plymouth Township issued a 12-page statement calling the challenge a blatant attempt to demand approval by tantrum, while council president Lynne Viscio says O’Neill bullied and intimidated township officials.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: The relationship has broken down publicly, which lengthens the timeline regardless of how the legal question resolves.
insights.quote: a blatant attempt by the Applicant to demand approval by tantrum. The Township will not entertain such theatrics.
insights.locator: On Monday night, Plymouth Township released a 12-page statement

insights.claim: O’Neill says he has already agreed to the majority of what the township wanted and asserts landowner rights, while acknowledging the township is under political scrutiny from residents and outsiders.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: The dispute is over a minority of conditions, so the outcome hinges on a few specific high-cost items like on-site power.
insights.quote: However, I am a landowner, and I do have rights, and it is their job to be impartial and fair in their analysis and response.
insights.locator: To O’Neill, all of this looks like an attempt

insights.claim: O’Neill hopes to build six data centers across the area, so the outcome of this single zoning fight determines the viability of a much larger regional pipeline.
insights.speaker: Nate Anderson
insights.so_what: One precedent-setting case gates a six-site pipeline; the ruling is a leveraged read on regional data center supply.
insights.quote: Success may turn on whether these township demands are normal zoning conditions designed to protect residents—or so onerous that they amount to prohibition by another name.
insights.locator: O’Neill hopes to build six data centers
